lesson.title: Meet a real table

lead.text: Start with what is inside the shop's file. It is plain text, with one order on each line and the values on a line separated by commas. The first line is different. It holds the names of the things recorded, such as shop, units and price. Everything after it is data. This layout is called a CSV file, short for “comma-separated values”, and almost every spreadsheet and database can produce one.

Open the file in a text editor and the first line reads shop,units,price. The second line reads Bay,2,5 and the third reads Hill,1,8. Each line after the first is one order, which makes it a row of the table. Each comma marks the edge between two values. All the unit counts together make a column. The first line is the header. It names the columns and is not an order itself.

Lines of text cannot be added up or averaged until a program has split each line into its values. The pandas library does that. It is a Python library for tables, and by habit it is imported as pd. The call pd.read_csv("orders.csv") reads the header line and uses it for the column names, then turns every line below it into a row.

What comes back is a DataFrame, pandas' name for a table with named columns. Each column holds one kind of value and each row is one record, here one order. A file with a header and ten lines of orders gives a DataFrame with ten rows. The header became the column names, so it is not counted as data. By habit the DataFrame is stored in a name called df, and the rest of this lesson does the same.
The header names the columns. Think about which lines of the file turn into rows.

Once a table is in, the first thing to find out is how big it is. A DataFrame reports that through its shape, a pair of numbers with the rows first and the columns second. The shop's table has four orders and three columns, so df.shape is (4, 3).

To pick out one column, put its name in square brackets. df['units'] gives the four unit counts as a Series, which is a single column of values with the row numbers beside it. Putting the name in a list, df[['units']], gives a DataFrame that happens to have one column. The two print in a similar way and have different shapes.
Step through the figure for the four-order table. The first case picks the column by its name alone and the second picks it with a list.

afterFigure.text: The Series has the shape (4,), a single number, because it has only one direction to count along. The one-column DataFrame has the shape (4, 1), which is four rows and one column. The rule to keep is that a single name gives a Series and a list of names gives a DataFrame.

cases.label: Case A
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({
    'shop': ['Bay', 'Hill', 'Bay', 'Hill'],
    'units': [2, 1, 3, 4],
    'price': [5, 8, 5, 8]
})
result = df['units']
shape = df.shape

cases.label: Case B
cases.code:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({
    'shop': ['Bay', 'Hill', 'Bay', 'Hill'],
    'units': [2, 1, 3, 4],
    'price': [5, 8, 5, 8]
})
result = df[['units']]
shape = result.shape

steps.headline: A table has 6 rows and the columns shop, units and price. What are the shapes of df, df['units'] and df[['units']]?

lead.text: Apply the rule to a longer table.

workedSteps.text: A single name gives a Series: one axis of 6 values.
A list of names keeps a table with that column only.

steps.headline: A DataFrame has shape (7, 3). How many columns does df have, and how many does df[['units']] have?

workedSteps.text: Shape gives rows first, then columns. How many columns does df have?
A list of one name keeps a table with one column. How many columns does df[['units']] have?

lead.text: A real file can have thousands of rows, and printing them all only buries the part you need. df.head(4) returns the first four rows, which is enough to see what the table holds. With no number it returns five. The result is a preview. It is a separate object, so the table you asked about is untouched, and a table with ten rows still has ten rows after you store first_rows = df.head(4).

Shape and head together make a quick check after every read. Shape says whether the table has the size you expected. Head shows whether each column holds what its name promises. A problem is far cheaper to fix at this point than after an hour of analysis built on top of it.

Now back to the code 0012. When read_csv reads a column it guesses what kind of value is in it. A column made only of digits is taken to hold numbers, and a number is stored without leading zeros, so 0012 becomes 12. Each column has a dtype, short for data type, that says what kind of value it holds. df.dtypes lists them, and a column of whole numbers shows as int64.

A product code is a label and not a quantity. Nobody adds two codes together, and the zeros are part of the label. You can tell read_csv to keep the column as text with dtype={'code': 'str'}. Text keeps every character that was written, so 0012 stays 0012. Check df.dtypes after reading, because it shows at once when a column has been turned into something you did not intend.
A code is a label and not a quantity. Decide how the column should be read.
Text keeps every character that was written, so the length of a code is the number of characters in it.

steps.headline: When the commas are not commas

lead.text: The shop's second branch exports its file differently. The values on each line are separated by semicolons. read_csv splits at commas unless it is told otherwise, and a semicolon file read that way finds no commas to split at. Each whole line stays in one cell, and the table comes out with a single column holding text like Bay;2;5.

The separator is set with the sep argument. pd.read_csv("branch2.csv", sep=";") splits at the semicolons and gives the three columns the file really has. This is one more reason to check shape straight after reading. A table with the right number of rows and only one column is the sign of a wrong separator, and you can see it before any calculation runs on the wrong table.
read_csv splits at commas by default. Think about what the lines of a semicolon file contain.

lesson.orientation: Read CSV data, inspect a DataFrame and preserve meaningful column types.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea with a new input.

blocks.text: Every Monday a shop emails a file of last week's orders. Someone opens it in a spreadsheet to have a look, and one product code stands out: the code 0012 now shows as 12. The spreadsheet decided that the cell held a number, and numbers have no use for leading zeros, so it dropped them without a word.

A program that reads the file can make the same slip, so the first job with any new file is to check what actually arrived. The checks are short. Count the rows and columns, and see whether any value changed on the way in, as the code 0012 did.
This lesson follows one weekly file from the moment it is read to the moment you can trust it.

intro.promise: By the end you'll read a CSV into a DataFrame, read its shape, and keep identifier codes from turning into numbers.

recap.keyIdea: read_csv turns lines into rows under a header, shape gives rows then columns, head previews without changing the table, and codes and separators have to be read as they were written.

blocks.text: You saw 0012 turn into 12 in a spreadsheet cell. You counted 6 rows below a header, kept all 4 characters of a code by reading it as text, and found that a semicolon file read with commas has 1 column.

recap.nextHook: With the table in, the next job is to pick out the row you mean. Every row carries a label, much as a locker has a number on its door, and that label can differ from the place where the row stands. The next lesson tells labels from positions and shows how to pick rows with each.

questions.prompt: A CSV has one header line followed by six data lines, with no blank lines. How many DataFrame rows are read?
hints: The header is not an observation.
The header becomes the column names.
Count the data lines after the header.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The header supplies column names, leaving six data rows.

questions.onCorrect: 6. The header became the column names, so only the six data lines are rows.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts the header line. It becomes column names, not a row.

questions.prompt: How many columns does df have when its shape is (7, 3)?
hints: Shape gives rows first.
Read the second entry of the shape.
The second entry counts columns.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The second shape entry is the column count, so there are three columns.

questions.onCorrect: 3. Shape lists rows, then columns, so the second entry is the column count.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the row count, the first entry.

questions.prompt: How should an ID such as 0012 be read when its leading zeros matter?
hints: Is an identifier a quantity or a label?

acceptedIdeas: As text, with an explicit string dtype
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: An explicit string dtype preserves the ID's characters, including leading zeros.

choices.label: As text, with an explicit string dtype
As an integer, then divided by ten

questions.onCorrect: As text, with an explicit string dtype. That keeps every character, including leading zeros.

misconceptions.feedback: A float is a measurement and would lose the zeros.
Arithmetic on an identifier is meaningless and does not restore the zeros.

questions.prompt: A semicolon-separated file has four columns. It is read with read_csv and no sep argument. How many columns does the DataFrame have?
hints: What does read_csv split at by default?
The lines contain no commas.
Nothing was split, so how many columns is that?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: No commas means no splits, so there is one column.

questions.onCorrect: 1. With no commas to split at, every line stayed whole in a single column.

misconceptions.feedback: The columns would be separated only with sep=';'. The default looks for commas.

questions.prompt: A DataFrame has eight rows. How many rows does df.head(3) return?
hints: head selects a preview.
There are enough rows for the preview.
head takes the number of rows you ask for.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: head(3) returns the first three rows without removing the remaining rows.

questions.onCorrect: 3. head returns the first rows you ask for, without removing the others.

misconceptions.feedback: head returns only a preview, not the whole table.

questions.prompt: A DataFrame has five rows. How many rows remain in df after preview = df.head(2)?
hints: A returned object is separate from df.
The preview is a separate selection.
No line replaces or edits df itself.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Creating the preview does not mutate df; all five rows remain.

questions.onCorrect: 5. The preview is a new object, and df itself is not changed.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the preview. df keeps all its rows.

hints: sep tells read_csv where to split.
Each field between semicolons is a column.
Count the fields in the header.
questions.prompt: A semicolon-separated file has four columns. It is read with sep=';'. How many columns does the DataFrame have?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Each of the four fields becomes a column.

questions.onCorrect: 4. Splitting at the semicolons gives one column for each field.

misconceptions.feedback: That is what happens without sep. With sep=';' the lines are split.

hints: A number has no leading zeros.
The cell stores a quantity, not characters.
Write the code as an ordinary number, without padding.
questions.prompt: What number does the cell show?
questions.onCorrect: 12. A number format drops leading zeros. read_csv does the same unless you tell it that the column is text.

misconceptions.feedback: Only the padding zeros disappear. The other digits stay.
Leading zeros do not shift the remaining digits.

hints: Which line supplies the names of the columns?
questions.prompt: What does the first line of a CSV become when read with read_csv?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The header supplies the column names.

questions.onCorrect: The column names. The header is read as names, and the later lines become the rows.

misconceptions.feedback: The header gives names, not data, so the first data line is the second line.
The header is used, not ignored.

hints: What does the list of names do that a single name does not?
questions.prompt: Why is df['units'] a Series but df[['units']] a table?

choices.label: A single name gives one column; a list of names keeps a table

acceptedIdeas: A single name gives one column; a list of names keeps a table
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: A list of names keeps the result a DataFrame.

questions.onCorrect: A single name gives one column, while a list of names keeps a table.

misconceptions.feedback: Brackets select, they do not sort.
Both hold the same four values. They differ in shape.

hints: How many names are in the list?
Each name keeps one column.
Count the names.
questions.prompt: How many columns does df[['units']] have?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: One name in the list keeps one column.

questions.onCorrect: 1. A list of one name keeps a table with that single column.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the column count of the whole table. The list names only one column.

hints: Text keeps every character that was written.
Leading zeros are characters too.
Count the characters in 0012.
questions.prompt: A code column is read with dtype str. How many characters does the code 0012 keep?
questions.onCorrect: 4. As text, 0012 keeps all four characters, zeros included.

misconceptions.feedback: That counts only the digits left after dropping the zeros. As text they are kept.
